notes.b: Achievement is the result of a student's ability combined with the effort, attitude and health they bring to learning. Ability is only one factor among several, so two students of equal ability can get very different results.
points: Intellectual ability (intelligence) affects how quickly a student learns and the level at which they can perform, but ability alone does not decide results, because work and support matter too.
Learning difficulties, such as dyslexia (a difficulty with reading and spelling), can lower achievement if the student is not supported.
Work ethic, meaning commitment to homework, revision, attendance and class participation, has a direct effect on results because learning builds up through regular practice.
Attitude and motivation matter: a student who values learning and sets personal goals tends to achieve more, while one who sees school as pointless will often disengage.

Poor health, including illness, tiredness, lack of sleep and poor nutrition, reduces concentration and attendance, so the student misses or fails to take in lessons. Mental health and stress matter too.
Choosing subjects and a level that match a student's interests and abilities improves engagement and results. At third level, choosing the wrong course can lead to poor results or dropping out.
Part-time work during term time (at second and third level) reduces study time and can leave a student tired in class.
notes.tip: Exams ask for three or four factors, each with a reason. For each one, say how it raises or lowers achievement, because a factor with no effect stated earns no marks. Treat intelligence as one factor among several, never the only cause.

notes.b: A student's family shapes their expectations, their resources and the conditions in which they study. Some of these influences come from the family's attitudes, others from money and circumstances.
points: Parental attitude: parents who value education, take an interest in homework and school, and have high expectations tend to raise their child's achievement.
Parents' own level of education shapes the expectations they hold for their children, their understanding of the school system and how much help they can give with schoolwork and choices.
Family size: in larger families, parents' time, attention and money for each child are often more limited, and older children may have caring duties.

Family finances and socio-economic background affect access to books, uniform, a computer, extra tuition, school trips and activities. They can also decide whether a student must work part-time or leave school early.

Home environment: a quiet place to study, books, a computer and internet access, a routine for homework and the absence of overcrowding all support homework and revision. Without them, study is difficult.
Family circumstances such as separation, bereavement, illness, addiction in the home, conflict or unemployment cause stress that can lower concentration and attendance.
A cycle of poverty and low expectations can pass down through generations, because children who see little value in education may carry the same expectations into their own lives.
notes.tip: Keep family factors under clear headings, such as parental attitude, finances, family size and home environment. For home environment, be ready to name three home conditions that help study, for example a quiet space, books and internet access.

notes.b: Students spend much of the day with people their own age, so the peer group (the friends and classmates a student mixes with) has a strong influence on how they behave in school.
points: Positive peers encourage effort and study, because students tend to copy the behaviour of the group they belong to.
Negative peer pressure encourages truancy (staying away from school without permission), disruption and early leaving, so a student can disengage in order to fit in.
Bullying damages self-confidence and can cause a student to miss school or stop engaging with learning.
notes.tip: Short questions ask for two effects of bullying or poor health on achievement. Give a clear effect each time, such as lost confidence, missed school or poor concentration.

notes.b: The school a student attends affects what they can learn and how they feel about learning. Both the atmosphere of the school and the resources it has to work with count.
points: School attended and environment: the school's ethos (its values and outlook), discipline, atmosphere and expectations of its pupils, together with the range of subjects offered and whether it is single-sex or mixed. A supportive, safe environment helps achievement.
Teacher expectations shape pupils' attainment, because low expectations of a student can limit the goals they set themselves. Teacher quality also affects how well students learn.
School resources, including class size, access to technology and equipment, laboratories, libraries and a guidance counsellor, affect what students can learn.
Supports such as learning support teachers, special needs assistants (SNAs) and exam accommodations help pupils with special needs to achieve.
notes.tip: A strong answer on school factors names specific resources, for example class size, technology, teacher expectations and supports for special needs, and says how each one affects results.

notes.b: Where a school is, how often a student attends, and the supports on offer all affect results. Poor attendance in particular leaves gaps that are hard to close.
points: The locality of a school matters: schools in socially disadvantaged areas often face higher rates of early school leaving, fewer after-school facilities and less access to resources.
Students may also live far from school or lack transport, which can hurt attendance. Good local amenities, libraries and community supports help.
Poor school attendance leads to gaps in learning and lower attainment, and it is linked with early school leaving.

Programmes and supports can raise achievement for students who might otherwise drop out: Transition Year, LCA, LCVP, JCSP, work experience, access routes to third level (such as HEAR and DARE) and exam accommodations (RACE).
notes.tip: Treat programmes as supports, not as a list of schemes to describe: give the name in a clause and say how it helps. Give locality, attendance and family finances as factors with an effect, and leave wider discussions of inequality for where they are asked.

notes.b: Many of the same factors apply to students in college, though the details change because students are older and often live away from home.
points: Correct choice of course matters, because the wrong course can lead to poor results or dropping out.
Cost of fees, accommodation and travel, together with family situation, can limit what a student can afford, so working part-time may be needed, which cuts study time.
Home and college environment affect study: a student needs a suitable place to work and a college that supports them.
Positive or negative peers influence a student's effort, and parental attitude still affects their motivation.
Locality and distance from home affect travel time and cost, and college supports help students who are struggling.
Ability and work ethic remain key, because college students must study independently.
notes.tip: The third-level version asks for four factors. Good ones are course choice, cost and part-time work, home and college environment, peers and parental attitude, each with its effect.

keyTerms.definition: A student's capacity to learn, reason and understand, which influences the pace and level of their learning.
A student's commitment to completing homework, revision and class tasks conscientiously.
The value parents place on education and the interest and support they show in their child's schoolwork.
The physical and emotional conditions at home, including study space, resources and family stability, that support or hinder learning.
The influence of a student's friends and classmates on their behaviour, effort and choices.
Absence from school without a valid reason.
Repeated, deliberate behaviour that hurts or intimidates another person, carried out by one student or group against another.
The number of pupils for each teacher in a school or class, which affects how much individual attention each pupil receives.
The social and economic character of the area a school serves, which can affect resources and student outcomes.

factCards.term: Four family influences on a child's achievement
factCards.definition: Parental attitude, parents' own education, family size and family finances.

factCards.term: Three home conditions that support homework and revision
factCards.definition: A quiet place to study, books, and internet access.

factCards.term: Two effects of poor health on a student
Two ways a peer group can affect effort
factCards.definition: Positive peers encourage study; negative peer pressure can lead to truancy and disengagement.

factCards.definition: It damages self-confidence and can cause the student to miss school or disengage from learning.

factCards.term: Two school-level factors that affect learning
factCards.definition: Class size and access to technology.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which a student's home environment can affect their results at school.
questions.model: Any two, three marks each: a quiet place to study, books and internet access support homework and revision; family finances determine access to resources and extra tuition; parental attitude and interest in schoolwork encourage effort; family disruption such as separation or bereavement causes stress that lowers concentration and attendance.

questions.prompt: Explain how individual, family and school factors each affect how well a student performs at school.
questions.model: Individual: intellectual ability affecting pace and level of learning; work ethic and commitment to homework and revision; attitude and goal setting; health affecting concentration and attendance; subject choice matched to interests and abilities; part-time work reducing study time. Family: parental attitude and interest; parents' own education and expectations; family size limiting time and money per child; finances affecting books, computers and tuition; home study facilities; family disruption causing stress. School: peer groups encouraging or discouraging effort; negative peer pressure and truancy; bullying damaging confidence and attendance; school locality in a socially disadvantaged area and higher early school leaving; class size and pupil-teacher ratio affecting individual attention; quality of resources, technology and teacher expectations.
